title: Male privilege: things I can do, but many women can’t
excerpt: Male privilege is not always about what men receive. Sometimes it is about what men never have to worry about. A reflection on everyday freedoms and responsibility.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Everyday freedoms I rarely notice","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I have been reflecting on male privilege, particularly in today’s climate of increasing misogyny, sexual harassment and violence against women and girls.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"As a man, there are everyday freedoms I rarely stop to appreciate. I can leave my house at 2am, walk down the street or catch public transport without routinely planning my journey around the possibility of being followed, harassed or sexually assaulted.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I can walk past a group of strangers without anticipating catcalling, unwanted comments about my body or intimidating behaviour.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I can get on a train or a bus without worrying about being groped or sexually assaulted, or having to think about where I sit, which carriage I use or how I will get home safely.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I can wear whatever colour clothing I want without worrying about my period starting unexpectedly and leaving a visible stain.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I can spend a day in an office without routinely fearing that someone might proposition me, make misogynistic comments, objectify my body or grope me.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Male privilege isn’t always about what men receive. Sometimes it’s about what men don’t have to worry about.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"quote","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Identities intersect","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"As a Black man, I understand discrimination and the assumptions that come with my identity. But experiencing racism doesn’t mean I cannot also benefit from male privilege. Our identities intersect, and our experiences are not interchangeable.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"What concerns me is how often women are told to change their behaviour rather than society challenging the behaviours that threaten their safety.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Why must women think about what they wear, where they go, what time they travel and how they get home? Why isn’t the same energy directed towards challenging the people who make these precautions necessary?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"What all men can do","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Now, I do not believe every man is a perpetrator, but I do believe every man has a responsibility to challenge misogyny.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"That means:","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Calling out catcalling, sexual harassment and sexist jokes, including among our friends.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":1,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Understanding consent, boundaries and respect.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":2,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Taking disclosures of sexual assault seriously and rejecting victim-blaming.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":3,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Supporting women who speak up rather than becoming defensive.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":4,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"And raising boys and young men to understand accountability.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":5,"version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"listType":"bullet","start":1,"tag":"ul","type":"list","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I want women to enjoy the everyday freedoms I take for granted: walking home at night, travelling on public transport, choosing what to wear and going to work without constantly calculating risks to their safety.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"So, my fellow men, when was the last time you considered the things you can do without fear that the women in your life might think twice about? And what are you doing to change that?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Let’s move beyond saying “not all men” and start talking about what all men can do.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: “We’ll do it later”: the four most dangerous words in inclusion
excerpt: Inclusion work rarely gets cancelled. It gets postponed. Here is what “later” quietly costs a team, and why a busy period is exactly when it matters.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Why “later” feels reasonable","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I hear you, life is full-on, isn’t it.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"KPIs cha-cha-ing, inboxes breeding in the corner, hybrid teams struggling to remember what day it is they’re back in the office… Oh, and someone just said “budget cuts/re-structure” again. A fourth time.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The next thing you’re going to want to say is, “Let’s do this inclusion training later.”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Look, I get it. And I’m not saying training’s the magic wand. Inclusion needs to start at the top. But it also needs to happen at all levels. By everyone. And if you don’t do it now, when?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"What “later” actually costs","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Because the thing is, that “later” is where inclusion gaps start to form. And the productivity starts to fall, staff retention and all that money spent on it falls through the floor, oh and the employment tribunals start calling.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"When your people are stressed, exhausted, disconnected, that’s when trust erodes, bit by bit, quietly but surely. Exclusion creeps in, not because anyone’s being deliberately obtuse but because there’s no bandwidth left for empathy, no margin between Teams/Zoom calls and to-do lists.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Inclusion for the here and now","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"That’s why I designed “The Inclusive Practice Masterclass: Building Trust and Equity at Work”. A fast, high-impact training session that’s already been road-tested for the here and now, not the vague “when things calm down” (spoiler: they don’t).","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"You’ll get practical advice on:","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"How to spot and manage bias when it comes to actual decisions","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":1,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"How to tackle tricky conversations without making them 10x trickier","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":2,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"How to hold on to inclusion even when the deadline’s breathing down your neck","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":3,"version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"listType":"bullet","start":1,"tag":"ul","type":"list","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Because inclusion isn’t some airy-fairy “nice-to-have” add-on. Inclusion is the secret sauce that keeps your teams cohesive, creative, and let’s face it, human. Especially when times are hard.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Let’s make inclusion something your team does, not just talks about.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: Your hiring process might be costing you talent
excerpt: Unconscious bias hides in gut feelings and “culture fit”. Five simple ways to reduce it in your interviews, and why it matters to the bottom line.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Where bias hides","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"CEOs & CFOs: your hiring process might be costing you talent. And you might not even know it.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Unconscious bias doesn’t usually walk into the interview room wearing a badge saying “Hello, I’m bias… Nice to meet you”. It hides in gut feelings, “culture fit”, CV preferences and those mysterious moments when someone says: “I just didn’t think they were the right fit.”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Five simple ways to reduce it","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Standardise your interview process. Same structure. Same expectations. Less room for personal preferences to sneak in.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":1,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Use structured questions. Stop letting interviews become competitive storytelling sessions. Ask candidates the same core questions and assess the answers consistently.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":2,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Use diverse interview panels. Different perspectives can challenge assumptions that one person might not even realise they’re making.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":3,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Focus on objective criteria. Score against the skills, experience and behaviours actually needed for the role, not whether you’d enjoy having them in the pub.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":4,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Educate your hiring team. You can’t manage the bias you don’t understand. Give managers the knowledge and tools to recognise and challenge it.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":5,"version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"listType":"number","start":1,"tag":"ol","type":"list","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Why this is a business issue","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"For CEOs and CFOs, this isn’t just about being “nice” or ticking the DEI box. Better hiring decisions mean access to a wider talent pool, stronger teams and fewer expensive recruitment mistakes.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Because “they just didn’t feel like the right fit” isn’t exactly a robust business case.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Ask yourself: is your recruitment process selecting the best person for the job, or the person who feels most familiar?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: “This is not a costume. It’s my cultural attire.”
excerpt: A costume is something you wear to pretend. Culture is what you wear to be. On cultural and religious dress, microaggressions and inclusive dress codes.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Sunday at church","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"On Sunday, I went to church wearing my traditional cultural attire that represents my Igbo heritage, and I must say, some of the reactions I got both angered and saddened me.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"My experience made me realise that, from turbans to hijabs, saris to Isiagu (Igbo cloth) and Kente (Ghanaian cloth), kilts to kippahs, cultural and religious attire tells stories that run deeper than the fabric.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"They speak of identity, belief, resistance, belonging, memory and pride. They are worn to honour ancestors, mark sacred traditions, and carry legacies forward, or as formal corporate attire.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Not dressing up","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"So, when I wear my cultural attire, I am not dressing up. brilliance.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"From comments to expression.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":1,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I think it is time to educate yourself and others.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":2,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I think it title: Growing up Chuks
excerpt: If you grow up disabled in Nigeria, two things are certain: you learn that survival is a skill, and you develop a dark sense of humour. A personal story of family, Lagos and belonging.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Seen first","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"If you grow up disabled in Nigeria, two things are certain. First, you’ll learn that survival is a skill. Second, you’ll develop a black sense of humour.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I was one of the lucky ones. My family love me for who I am. That’s not to say they didn’t see my disability, it’s just that they saw me first. I know for some families, a child with a disability is something to be ashamed of or even kept a secret. So, in many ways, having a Mum and Dad, and three brothers who simply saw me before they saw my disability, was ground-breaking. They taught me to dream big and that I could do anything. Well, apart from climbing mango trees… my mum still won’t let me forget that.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The world outside the family home","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Schools, buses, the mean streets of Lagos. Navigating the world outside the family home was a different story. Public attitudes and perceptions could turn a simple bus journey into an Olympic challenge.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"With educational doors being slammed in my face, I had to learn, from watching my Mum and Dad, to fight for what I wanted, sometimes loudly, sometimes by quietly and doggedly wearing people down. Fighting to get accepted into mainstream education despite having and sometimes surpassing the grades, fighting to be accepted by teachers and, yes, fellow pupils. I had to find ways to succeed and flourish in a system that was not designed for people like me.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Big business in Nigeria? I survived. Power suits and prejudice, I did both.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"My first job was as a TV presenter with the Nigerian Television Authority. I also had a lot of jokes and some damned good stubbornness (aka Chuksness).","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Coming back to the UK","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Returning to the UK later in life was… an experience, let’s say. Ramps! Accessible loos! People actually asking what support you might need, instead of having to tell them! But I will say, even here, despite the good intentions, genuine inclusion still has some distance to go to make it real.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The boy who wanted to belong","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"As I write this, I think about that British boy who grew up in Lagos and now lives in London, who just wanted to, and still wants to, belong, and how proud he’d be to see how far we as a society have come, and how much we’re still pushing forward.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Disability isn’t something to overcome. It’s part of who I am, a story I carry, laugh about, and use to open doors for others.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"quote","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: Dear designers: my missing arm is not the accessibility problem. Your building is.
excerpt: A heavy door, a badly laid out toilet and a café tray. A weekend out with one arm is a reminder that disability is often about how spaces are designed.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"A door, a tap and a tray","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"This weekend, I was out enjoying myself in the hot weather when I was reminded that the biggest barrier to disability isn’t my one arm… it’s whoever designed some of these public spaces.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"What happened, I hear you ask… well, I approached a door. It had one of those industrial-strength closers that seemed to have been borrowed from a bank vault.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Now, if you have got two hands, you pull with one and steady yourself with the other.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I have one arm.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"So for a brief moment, it looked less like I was entering a building and more like I was auditioning for Gladiators.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Then came the toilets…","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The soap dispenser needed one hand… The tap needed another… The paper towels were somewhere behind me. Whoever designed that layout clearly assumed we’d all arrive with spare limbs.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"And don’t get me started on carrying food and a drink… Apparently, some cafés still believe everyone was issued with two hands at birth.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"It’s the environment that struggles","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Here’s the thing, people often ask me, “What’s it like having one arm?”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Most days? Absolutely fine. It’s the environment that struggles, not me.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Disability isn’t always about our bodies. It is often about spaces that were designed with only one type of person in mind.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"One simple question","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The good news?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"These aren’t impossible problems to fix. They just require someone, somewhere, to ask one simple question:","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"What if the person using this only has one hand?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"quote","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"It is amazing how much more accessible the world becomes when we design for people instead of assumptions.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Now, if you’ll excuse me, I’m off to find a café where I can carry both my coffee and my dignity at the same time. 😂","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: “I was only joking”: the national anthem of workplace microaggressions
excerpt: Everyone chuckles except the person the joke was aimed at. Why microaggressions are never micro to the person on the receiving end, and what leaders can do.

Unchallenged, they fester and spread to become toxic to confidence, belonging, wellbeing and ultimately performance across your organisation.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"What you can do","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"So what can you do? You can:","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Teach colleagues how to confidently and respectfully challenge inappropriate behaviour with bystander intervention training.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":1,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Build clear, trusted routes for reporting incidents that people actually feel safe to use.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":2,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Embed a culture of accountability that rewards learning, apologising and improving, not going undetected.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":3,"version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"listType":"bullet","start":1,"tag":"ul","type":"list","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"A healthy workplace isn’t a place where nobody ever makes a mistake. It’s one where everyone knows how to put it right.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"If you’re not capturing what’s going on within your organisation, you’re leaving your DEI strategy up to chance. Hope is not a strategy, and hope has terrible reporting KPIs.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Let’s stop guessing and start measuring what matters.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: The power of a name in fostering belonging at work
excerpt: A name carries hopes, history and identity. Taking the time to say a colleague’s name correctly is a small act that says “I see you”.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"My name is Chukwunweike","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"My name is Chukwunweike Etuka. Chukwunweike is a name from the Igbo tribe in Eastern Nigeria. Translated, it means “God has Power”. But you can call me Chuks… everyone calls me Chuks (apart from my parents, who call my full name when I have been naughty 🤣). It is the short form for Chukwunweike. It is not spelt “Chucks”, “Chuck”, “Chiks”, “Tuks” or “Chooooks”. It is simply Chuks.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"More than a label","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Have you ever stopped to think about the simple act of saying someone’s name correctly? In our diverse workplaces, a name is so much more than just a label. A deeply thought-out name is a representation of the hopes, dreams and aspirations the child’s parents or guardians have for their newly born baby.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"In some communities, the name given to a newborn represents the social standing of not only the child but the family. In some families, the name given to a newborn child is a prayer for success from the parents or guardians over the life of the child. In fact, a name is an essential part of our identity and a key to belonging.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“I see you”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"When we take the time to learn and pronounce a colleague’s name correctly, we’re not only showing respect, we’re also recognising and valuing their unique cultural background and personal story. It creates an environment where everyone feels seen, appreciated, and connected. It says “I see you”.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Respecting names builds trust and opens the door to more authentic communication. It can be as simple as asking, “Could you please teach me the correct pronunciation of your name?” or taking the initiative to learn it on your own. This small gesture can have a big impact on how individuals feel within the team. It reinforces their value and helps foster a culture of inclusion and mutual respect.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Start with names","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"As a manager, organisational leader and a member of society, I like to take the time to learn how to correctly pronounce the names of my colleagues, teammates and people I come across. That sense of belonging and look of appreciation on their faces when they hear their names correctly pronounced (even with inflections) is priceless, and that leads to a true sense of loyalty.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Let’s make it a point to celebrate our differences, starting with something as fundamental as names. By doing so, we pave the way for richer interactions, better collaboration, and a workplace where everyone feels they truly belong.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: Dear Google Maps: I am not a mountain goat
excerpt: Walking directions that end in a bush trail are an inconvenience for some and a dead end for others. A letter on why accessibility has to cover the whole journey.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"First, thank you","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Dear Google Maps Platform & Citymapper,","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Firstly, thank you. No clear path. Just a dense bush trail that felt less “walking directions” and more “I hope you packed supplies.”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Now, I got there (thank God). I am a capable human who can walk, balance, step over roots, and improvise. But that’s when my appreciation for your service turned into a very serious question: What if I had mobility issues? What if I was using a wheelchair? A walking aid? Had limited balance?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"How exactly would I have arrived at my destination, let alone for something as important and emotionally heavy as a funeral?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Naturally I checked my settings (because surely this was user error?). But I couldn’t find a setting that says:","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“Please do not send me through bushes.”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":1,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“Accessibility first, always.”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":2,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“End-to-end routes that assume I am human, not a mountain goat.”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":3,"version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"listType":"bullet","start":1,"tag":"ul","type":"list","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Accessibility as the default lens","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Accessibility options are there, but they don’t seem to shape the entire journey end to end by default. And that’s the issue. Access shouldn’t just disappear at the last 200 metres.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"This isn’t a tech rant. It’s a gentle nudge from someone who spends their working life thinking about inclusion: design choices quietly decide who gets where and who doesn’t.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"So here’s my humble request to the Map gods: let accessibility be a default lens, not an optional extra buried three menus deep. Because everyone deserves to arrive without bushwhacking, especially on difficult days.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Warm regards,","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"A loyal user who would rather not be routed through nature again.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: Three small tweaks to make your job descriptions more inclusive
excerpt: Inclusive job descriptions are not about lowering the bar. They are about widening the door. Three easy adjustments to make before you hit “Post”.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Before you hit “Post”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Speaking as a manager who has spent many years trying to hire “the right fit” (and occasionally wondering why no one applied).","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"If recruitment is on your to-do list, here are three easy adjustments that make a big difference, without turning your JD into a manifesto.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"1. Tone down the superhero language","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Stop writing like you’re casting for the next 007. “Rockstar”, “ninja”, “dominant self-starter”… They sound exciting, but they also narrow who feels this role is for them. Clear, gender-neutral language means more people seeing themselves in the job.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"2. Lead with skills, not the shopping list of qualifications","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Requiring 10 qualifications, 20 years’ experience and “experience of a role that has existed for 5 years” is… ambitious. title: Skin in the game: what it really means to be an ally
excerpt: Allyship is not a badge or a hashtag. It means being willing to take risks and be uncomfortable, especially at work. Here is the difference between easy and real.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"More than a badge","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Allyship isn’t a badge or a statement or a hashtag or a one-time act of support during a themed month.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"In episode 3 of our podcast “Celebrating the Ordinary”, titled “Skin in the game”, my co-host Runa Uddin and I have an in-depth conversation with Laura Johnson, who is a mum in a mixed-race family, about what real allyship looks like, and it’s this:","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"True allyship means having skin in the game: being willing to take risks, to be uncomfortable, and to stand up even when it costs you something. Especially in the workplace.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"quote","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Easy versus hard","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Now hold on! Let’s think about this for a sec.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"It is easy to attend an inclusion webinar. It is harder to challenge a colleague’s biased comment in a leadership meeting.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":1,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"It is easy to celebrate diversity on social media through our posts and likes. It is harder to question why all the decision-makers at the table look the same.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":2,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"It is easy to mentor someone from an underrepresented group. It is harder to step back and make space for them to lead.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":3,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"It is easy to say, “we value diversity”. It is harder to call out bigotry, discrimination and workplace bullying.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":4,"version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"listType":"bullet","start":1,"tag":"ul","type":"list","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"In my opinion, allyship without action is performative. And performance, no matter how well-intentioned, doesn’t change structures.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"What true allyship is","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Amplifying voices, not speaking over them.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":1,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Taking on the emotional labour of calling things out, not leaving it to the marginalised and victimised.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":2,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Advocating for policy and cultural change, not just representation.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":3,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Accepting that being an ally isn’t about being “safe”, it’s about being accountable.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":4,"version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"listType":"bullet","start":1,"tag":"ul","type":"list","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"If you’re never uncomfortable, never questioned, never at risk of losing social capital… then you might not have skin in the game yet.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"This isn’t about guilt. It’s about courage. Let’s move beyond optics and into action.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: Is your interviewee the diversity in the room?
excerpt: An interview for a DEI role, in front of a panel that looked like a photocopy of a photocopy. A reminder that the assessment goes both ways.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"A photocopy of a photocopy","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Picture this: you go for an in-person job interview, ready to bring your A-game, only to find yourself facing a panel of three that looks like a photocopy… of a photocopy… of the same person. All male, all white.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Well, this happened to me. And as someone sitting on the other side of the table (a position I am still not used to), companies need to realise: the assessment goes both ways.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"It was like they coordinated their wardrobes, facial expressions, and life experiences. You’re wondering if you accidentally walked into a historical reenactment of a 1980s boardroom meeting.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The questions","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"From the start, the interview was awkward… from their struggling to decide which hand to use to shake mine (left or right, believe me, it was a comical dance).","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"They started the interview with a classic: “Tell us about yourself.” And in my head, I am like: “Oh, you mean the part of me that stands out in this room right now?”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Next, I was asked the dreaded, “What would you bring to this role?” Translation: “How will you sprinkle some much-needed spice into this vanilla pudding of a team?”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Then I was asked, “How would you handle working with a diverse group of people?” To be honest with you, I was doing mental gymnastics trying not to laugh because… where are they, and why were none of them available for this interview?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"For me, the nail in the coffin was the question: “This role requires a lot of writing reports, email correspondence and developing presentations, how do you use a computer?” I must confess, that left me lost for words.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The real interview","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Let me tell you, the real interview wasn’t my answers, it was me figuring out whether to ask:","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“Do you have an inclusion strategy… or are you just winging it?”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":1,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“When was the last time you invited someone different to the table… or noticed their absence?”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":2,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"“You do know people living with disabilities exist in this world and I am not a figment of your collective imagination?”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":3,"version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"listType":"bullet","start":1,"tag":"ul","type":"list","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"But the kicker is, the interview was for a DEI role.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"What hiring managers should take from this","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Jokes aside, diversity isn’t just a buzzword; it’s the key to creativity, innovation, and better decision-making. If your interview panel looks like a line-up for a barbershop quartet, it might be time to shake things up.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"To all the companies out there: diversity in the room isn’t just about filling quotas, it’s about truly valuing different perspectives. And to my fellow interviewees: if you’re in this situation, don’t be afraid to be the voice that starts the conversation (or at least leaves them reflecting after you walk out!).","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The most diverse idea in the room shouldn’t be the candidate you’re interviewing.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"quote","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Let’s keep working toward interview panels that don’t look like they stepped out of a black-and-white photo!","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: Hidden workplace barriers: is your HR policy discriminating without you realising?
excerpt: Many HR policies create barriers nobody intended. The Bradford Factor is a clear example of an absence tool that penalises the people who most need flexibility.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Good values, harmful policies","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"This one is for HR department heads, HR managers, HR practitioners and HR consultants.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) are often championed in company values, yet many HR policies and practices continue to create systemic barriers for disabled employees and those from marginalised communities. In my opinion, no matter how many EDI policies and practices you put in place, while those barriers remain your staff retention rate will continue to tank.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"These barriers are not always intentional, but their impact is real and deeply felt. They often unintentionally discriminate against Black and Brown staff, new mothers, people living with disabilities, those with caring responsibilities and staff from marginalised communities, reinforcing systemic barriers rather than breaking them down.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"The Bradford Factor","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"One major example? The Bradford Factor: a rigid absence management tool that disproportionately penalises those who need flexibility the most.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"How does it harm marginalised employees (I hear you ask 😊)?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Neurodivergent employees who experience sensory overload or mental health crises are unfairly penalised instead of supported with reasonable adjustments.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":1,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Disabled staff and those with chronic illnesses such as epilepsy or sickle cell anaemia may require frequent short absences for medical appointments, yet this policy treats them as unreliable and, in some cases, lazy.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":2,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"New mums and caregivers, particularly in marginalised communities, often juggle extra responsibilities, from dealing with expensive childcare realities and supporting disabled family members to navigating healthcare disparities. A punitive approach only adds more pressure.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":3,"version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"listType":"bullet","start":1,"tag":"ul","type":"list","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Human-first, not numbers-driven","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Rather than enforcing rigid scoring systems, HR should prioritise inclusion, flexibility, and support over punishment. In fact, absence management should be human-first and not numbers-driven.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"It’s time to rethink policies that reinforce inequity.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: Why continually asking about adjustments matters
excerpt: Reasonable adjustments are not a one-time accommodation. Making them a standing item in every one-to-one keeps people supported as their needs change.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"A fixed item on the agenda","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"As a manager, I have monthly one-to-one meetings with all my direct reports and a fixed agenda item is a conversation about reasonable adjustments. My manager had the same agenda item in all my one-to-one meetings. It is through having these regular conversations I was provided with the appropriate tools and conducive workspace that enabled me to be my 100% productive self.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Inclusion isn’t just a buzzword; it isn’t just about one-time accommodations, it’s about ongoing dialogue and continuous improvement. Regularly checking in with staff about reasonable adjustments ensures that employees feel supported, valued, and empowered to do their best work. It enhances organisational culture, innovation, and performance.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Why the ongoing conversation matters","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Here’s why ongoing conversations about workplace adjustments matter:","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"An adapted workplace empowers everyone. A workplace that embraces reasonable adjustments such as ergonomic equipment, assistive technology, flexible work arrangements, and accessible spaces removes barriers and enables employees to thrive. When people have what they need, they bring their best selves to work, leading to increased engagement, productivity, and retention.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":1,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Needs change over time. Employees’ circumstances and needs evolve, whether due to a new diagnosis, changes in workload, or shifting work environments (e.g., hybrid or remote setups). Regular check-ins help identify new challenges before they become barriers.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":2,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"It encourages open conversations. By making it normal to discuss reasonable adjustments, organisations remove stigma and create a culture where employees feel safe to disclose their needs without fear of judgment.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":3,"version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"listType":"bullet","start":1,"tag":"ul","type":"list","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"An ongoing commitment","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Inclusion isn’t one-size-fits-all or one-and-done. Inclusion is an ongoing commitment. The question isn’t just, “Do we provide reasonable adjustments?” but rather, “Are we continuously adapting to meet the evolving needs of our team?”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"When was the last time your organisation asked, “Is there anything we can do to better support you?”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Let’s ensure accessibility and inclusion are woven into the fabric of our workplaces, not just as a requirement, but as a commitment to equity and belonging for all.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: Code-switching and disability: the silent workload we don’t talk about
excerpt: For many disabled professionals, code-switching is not about accent. It is the constant calculation of when to disclose, downplay or mask in order to fit in.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"What code-switching is","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Have you ever felt the need to adjust your accent, tone, or even personality to fit into a professional setting? That’s code-switching: the act of modifying speech, behaviour, or expression to conform to dominant workplace norms. For many, it’s an unspoken requirement to be perceived as “professional” or “a good fit.” But at what cost?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Code-switching can be exhausting.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"How it shows up for disabled professionals","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"For many disabled professionals, code-switching isn’t just about language, it’s about how we present our disabilities in the workplace. It’s the constant calculation of when to disclose, how to downplay, or whether to mask our pain, fatigue, or neurodivergence to fit in. It’s choosing between asking for the accommodations we need or pushing through to avoid being seen as “difficult.”","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"For people who society inappropriately describes as “socially awkward”, due to either being autistic or having Tourette syndrome, this hidden labour is exhausting. It creates anxiety, erodes confidence, and limits career progression. No one should feel pressure to perform able-bodiedness or filter their lived experience just to be accepted at work.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"When employees feel the pressure to mask aspects of their identity, we lose out on diverse perspectives, creativity, and true inclusion.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"What workplaces can do instead","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Instead of expecting employees to adapt to rigid workplace norms, we should be asking: how can we create environments where people feel valued just as they are, and disabled employees don’t feel the need to code-switch?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"We need to:","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Normalise accommodations. Support shouldn’t be seen as a special favour but as a right.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":1,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Redefine professionalism. Challenge outdated biases around energy levels, communication styles, accents, accessibility needs and cultural expressions. They vary, so respect that.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":2,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Foster psychological safety. Employees should feel comfortable and safe to be their authentic selves and open about their needs without fear of judgement or bias.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":3,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Lead with empathy. Assume competence, listen without judgment, and create spaces where difference is valued.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":4,"version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Listen and learn. Encourage open conversations about workplace culture and unconscious bias.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"listitem","value":5,"version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"listType":"bullet","start":1,"tag":"ul","type":"list","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"An inclusive workplace isn’t one where disabled employees must adapt to fit in. It’s one where the environment adapts to include them.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}

title: The intersectionality principle: why it matters at work
excerpt: Inclusion efforts that focus on one aspect of identity miss the people living at the overlaps. Three reasons an intersectional lens matters for employers.
body: {"root":{"children":[{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"What intersectionality means","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"As someone who navigates multiple identities, I’ve realised how important intersectionality is, not just as a concept, but as a lived experience. Intersectionality highlights how different aspects of our identity (race, gender, disability, sexuality, class, etc.) overlap to shape our experiences, opportunities, and challenges at work.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"For employers, fostering an inclusive and equitable workplace isn’t just about ticking diversity boxes, it’s about truly understanding the intersectionality of your employees’ identities and how that shapes their experiences at work. My experiences aren’t just influenced by being a man, but also by my ethnicity, disability and other identity factors. Inclusion efforts that focus on only one aspect of diversity often miss the unique challenges people like me face.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"So why does this matter?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Because representation alone isn’t enough","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I’ve been in spaces where diversity was celebrated, but my specific challenges, shaped by the intersections of my identity, weren’t always acknowledged. True inclusion means embracing complexity. Treating everyone the same isn’t enough (because we cannot truly treat everyone the same 😊). True inclusivity means recognising that different employees face different barriers and providing tailored support to ensure everyone has the same opportunities to thrive.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Because policies must reflect real experiences","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Flexible working policies, leadership programmes, and wellbeing initiatives should be designed with intersectionality in mind. What works for me as a Black man may not fully work for me as a person living with a disability or any other identity variable. Recruitment, promotions, and workplace policies must be reviewed through an intersectional lens, so they aren’t disadvantaging certain groups.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"Because everyone deserves to be seen and heard","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"heading","version":1,"tag":"h2"},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"When workplaces embrace intersectionality, employees feel safe, supported, and valued, empowering them to be their authentic selves. This boosts engagement, reduces turnover, and enhances an employer’s reputation. True inclusion drives a stronger, more successful workforce.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"I’ve worked in spaces that embrace intersectionality, where I can be comfortable enough to present the entirety of my Chuksness, but more is needed. Leaders must go beyond DEI&B checkboxes, driving real change so every employee can thrive barrier-free.","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1},{"children":[{"detail":0,"format":0,"mode":"normal","style":"","text":"An intersectional approach isn’t just the right thing to do, it’s essential for a thriving, innovative, and fair workplace. How are you embedding intersectionality into your workplace culture?","type":"text","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"paragraph","version":1}],"direction":null,"format":"","indent":0,"type":"root","version":1}}
